On 15.7.87, Mr. Hafizullah, the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 1 petitioner, filed the above application for returning the plaint to the plaintiff, but unfortunately this application was not heard during last three years. In the instant application, the learned Advocate submits that the present suit by the Insurer under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act is not maintainable. It is submitted that the Insurer is neither the owner nor the assignee nor the consignee of the goods imported. No damage was caused to the imported goods of the plaintiff and that since the owner of the vessel is Bangladeshi, the plaintiff being insurer cannot invoke the jurisdiction of the Admiralty-Court under section 6 of the Admiralty Court Act of 1861. 

 5. Mr. Manjur-ur-Rahim, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff, has filed a written objection against the aforesaid application filed under Order 7, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure denying the material allegations made in the application. It is his case that if the provisions of the section of Admiralty Court Act, 1861, are considered together, it appears that the Insurer is competent to file a suit under section 6 of the said Act. 

 6. In support of his contention Mr. Hafizullah has referred to the case of Al-Sayer Navigation Co. Vs. Delta International Traders Ltd. 34 DLR (AD), 110; Albert David (Bangladesh) Ltd. Vs. Mls. Nedlloyed Lijnel BV Rotterdam, 34 DLR 356 and Kings Shipping Traders Vs. M/s. LS Line and others, 38 DLR 30.  7. In the other case reported in 34 DLR 356 the learned Company Judge had considered the question of maintainability of admiralty suit before this Court after discussing in details the history of this Admiralty jurisdiction and held as follows : 

 "So far as the present action for non-delivery of the plaintiffs cargo is concerned thus jurisdiction of this Court is not derived from the Letters Patent of 1862 or that of 1865, but from the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act (India) of 1891 and the Courts of Admiralty Act, 1861 of England. The later Act is not on our statute book but it is administered in view of the combined operation of sub-section (2) of Section 2 of the Colonial Courts of Admiralty Act, 1890 of the British Parliament and the Colonial Court of Admiralty Act (India) 1891, the later Act being revised by the Bangladesh Laws (Revision and Declaration) Act, 1973 (Act VIII of 1973) is now on our statute book. It is true that if revised Court of Admiralty Act of 1891 is read in isolation then it would not give any idea as to the nature and extent of the Admiralty jurisdiction of this Court, but it is to be read in its historical perspective. Under the Act of 1891 the High Court Division of this Court was declared as the Court of Admiralty. This Court exercises the same jurisdiction as the High Court of England exercised in 1890 under the Admiralty Court Act of 1861." 

 8. In the case reported in 38 DLR his Lordship also held the similar view that this Court exercises the same jurisdiction as the High Court of England exercised in 1890 under the Admiralty Court Act of 1861. The upshot of the above decisions comes to this that section 6 of the Act is attracted only when damage is caused to the goods on board due to negligence, misconduct or breach of contract or breach of duty in relation to the goods.  13. Mr. Manjur-ur-Rahim, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff, has referred to the case of Bengal Liner Ltd. Vs. Sadharan Bima Corporation and another, reported in 1990 BLD, 105. I have carefully perused the above judgment. But, it appears to me that the facts and circumstances of that case are quite distinguishable from those of the instant  one. In that case Mr. Manjur-ur-Rahim was also the learned Advocate for the defendant No. 1 and he raised objection to the effect that the said suit arose out of an insurance claim and as such it would not fall within sections 6 and 7 or any other provisions of the Admiralty Court Act, 1861. In that case, the insurer was not the plaintiff. It has not been decidedin that case as to whether a suit would lie before the Admiralty Court if the goods are carried by a vessel belonging to a national of Bangladesh. In this view of the matter, I find that the above decision cited by Mr. Manjur-ur-Rahim is not of any assistance for the present case.
